source.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
source.authors: Dan Braun; Lucius Bushnaq; S. Heimersheim; Jake Mendel; Lee Sharkey

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests superposition and overlapping computations in toy networks using parameter decomposition and ablation, rather than the original neuron-visualization approach. These results bear conceptually on V3, but do not test polysemanticity in real vision or language models.
record.gate_note: The paper directly studies a toy model of superposition and toy networks computing more input-feature functions than they have MLP neurons. It reports neuron-contribution visualizations and ablations of decomposed parameter components. It does not test whether InceptionV1 neurons respond to unrelated image inputs, language-model neuron polysemanticity, or the other listed versions. Target-model performance and the hand-coded gated-function experiment do not measure neuron polysemanticity and are left out.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It assumes superposition and compressed computation in toy networks and reports how well its own APD decomposition recovers known mechanisms (MMCS, ML2R, scrubbing ablations). It does not measure how often neurons are polysemantic, and it does not compare conditions such as capacity, architecture or activation function that would test whether superposition causes polysemanticity. The target networks are built to compute 100 functions with 50 neurons. Neurons serving multiple features is therefore a premise of the setup, not a tested result.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that APD recovers ground-truth mechanisms in toy models of superposition, compressed computation and cross-layer distributed representations. They add that computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity and attribution quality must be addressed before APD can be applied to real models.
record.recipe_differences: APD decomposes network parameters and uses gradient attributions, top-k component selection, and a simplicity loss; it is not the original source's neuron-response visualization approach.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to hyperparameters, especially loss coefficients and, to a lesser extent, batch top-k. In the compressed-computation analyses, changing batch top-k changes whether computations are split across components or multiple input-feature computations are combined. Small hidden dimensions make the TMS5−2 setup brittle.

fits_no_version.finding: In a residual MLP trained to compute 100 ReLU functions with 50 neurons, target neurons contribute to several input-feature computations. APD recovers per-function parameter components that span those shared neurons (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computations sharing neurons in compressed-computation toy models can be separated into per-function parameter components.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to toy networks. The TMS5−2 setting is brittle, APD is hyperparameter-sensitive, some learned components are shrunk or partially represent secondary computations, and the neuron-contribution figures do not provide numerical estimates of overlap. The paper states that APD is not yet suitable for real-world models because of computational cost and other practical limitations.
record.rows_left_out: Left out target-model task-performance results, general APD mechanism visualizations, and the hand-coded gated-function model because they do not directly measure neuron polysemanticity or the superposition claim version. Other qualitative APD diagnostics are likewise omitted when they concern component recovery without a separately reported result bearing on V3.

untested.parts: No transformer language model neurons are studied.
Superposition is assumed in toy models. There is no test of whether it causes polysemanticity, e.g. no comparison of feature count against neuron count.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure is not examined.
No comparison of polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
Neuron-level classification criteria are not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests / T2' with V3 'supports' is reclassified. All rows evaluate the APD method or illustrate the designed premise, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or neuron responses to image inputs are tested.
No transformer language models, tokens, or language contexts are tested.
The experiments use toy networks, not evidence that superposition causes polysemanticity in trained vision or language models; they do not quantify a general share of polysemantic neurons.
The paper does not test polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
No comparison of neuron-polysemanticity shares across activation functions, architectures, or regularization is reported, nor a performance-cost evaluation of reducing that share.
The paper does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons with tools intended to find a shared feature.
The paper varies APD settings such as batch top-k, but does not test how neuron-polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: TMS5−2
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean max cosine similarity between target weight columns and their best-matching APD component columns.
rows.measure: MMCS of target model weight columns and APD components
rows.note: Authors say the near-1 MMCS indicates that the learned components are geometrically close to the target model weights. APD attributions in this setting were taken from the APD model rather than the target model.
rows.check: MMCS measures how closely APD components match TMS weight columns. This is the study's own method performance, not neuron polysemanticity or its cause.

rows.subject: TMS5−2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the ratio of matching APD component-column magnitudes to target weight-column magnitudes.
rows.measure: ML2R of matching APD component columns to target model weight columns
rows.note: The authors interpret the below-1 ratio as shrinkage in the components.
rows.check: ML2R measures APD component shrinkage, which is method performance. 'Partial' does not reflect any V3 effect.

rows.subject: TMS40−10
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean max cosine similarity between target weight columns and their best-matching APD component columns.
rows.measure: MMCS of target model weight columns and APD components
rows.note: Authors say the near-1 MMCS indicates that the learned components are geometrically close to the target model weights.
rows.check: Same as R1, for TMS40-10: APD recovery quality, not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: TMS40−10
rows.operation_detail: Measured the ratio of matching APD component-column magnitudes to target weight-column magnitudes.
rows.measure: ML2R of matching APD component columns to target model weight columns
rows.note: The authors interpret the below-1 ratio as shrinkage in the components.
rows.check: Same as R2, for TMS40-10: APD shrinkage, not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: 1-layer residual MLP target model
rows.size_stated: Residual stream width 1000; MLP width 50; 100 input features
rows.operation_detail: Displayed per-neuron contribution values for input-feature computations.
rows.measure: Per-neuron contributions to each input-feature computation
rows.note: The text describes this target network as computing 100 functions with 50 neurons and says the target computations involve neurons used for multiple input features. The plotted contribution values themselves are not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: The figure shows target-model neurons contributing to several input-feature computations. The network is forced by design to compute 100 functions with 50 neurons. There is no comparison condition and no numeric rate, so this is an illustration of the premise, not a test of V3.

rows.subject: 2-layer residual MLP target model
rows.size_stated: Residual stream width 1000; 50 MLP neurons split as 25 per layer; 100 input features
rows.operation_detail: Displayed per-neuron contribution values for input-feature computations across the concatenated MLP layers.
rows.measure: Per-neuron contributions to each input-feature computation
rows.note: The plot shows contributions across both layers, but the text does not explicitly state a neuron-level overlap result for this figure; its plotted values are not given numerically.
rows.check: Figure-only neuron contributions in the 2-layer toy model. Same issue as R5, and the text states no overlap result for it.

rows.subject: APD-decomposed 1-layer residual MLP
rows.size_stated: Residual stream width 1000; MLP width 50; 100 input features; 130 parameter components initialized
rows.operation_detail: Ablated half of the parameter components while preserving components identified as responsible for the active inputs (scrubbed run).

conditions.value: half of components; component for active input preserved

rows.baseline: APD top-k sparse forward pass and target-model output are shown as references
rows.value: Scrubbed ablations perturb the output only slightly; MSE does not increase greatly.
rows.note: The paper reports that ablation of unrelated components has little effect compared with ablation of components responsible for active inputs.
rows.check: Scrubbed ablation of APD components validates the method's decomposition. It does not measure neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: APD-decomposed 1-layer residual MLP
rows.size_stated: Residual stream width 1000; MLP width 50; 100 input features; 130 parameter components initialized
rows.operation_detail: Ablated half of the parameter components, including components identified as responsible for the active inputs (anti-scrubbed run).

conditions.value: half of components; relevant component included among those ablated

rows.baseline: APD top-k sparse forward pass and target-model output are shown as references
rows.value: Ablating components responsible for the active inputs causes a large MSE increase.
rows.note: The text explicitly contrasts this result with the small effect of scrubbed ablations.
rows.check: Anti-scrubbed ablation is a method validation comparator, not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: APD-decomposed 2-layer residual MLP
rows.size_stated: Residual stream width 1000; 50 MLP neurons split as 25 per layer; 100 input features; 200 parameter components initialized
rows.operation_detail: Ablated half of the parameter components while preserving components identified as responsible for the active inputs (scrubbed run).

conditions.value: half of components; component for active input preserved

rows.baseline: APD top-k sparse forward pass and target-model output are shown as references
rows.value: Qualitatively similar to the 1-layer case; unrelated components have minimal influence when the corresponding input feature is not active.
rows.note: The authors describe the two-layer scrubbed/anti-scrubbed results as qualitatively similar to the one-layer results.

conditions.value: half of components; relevant component included among those ablated

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The TMS component-matching results and the target-model neuron-contribution and component-ablation results are consistent with distinct computations being packed into networks with a narrower hidden layer; see R1–R5 and R7–R10.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Quality and completeness of decomposition in the tested toy settings
reader_labels.reason: The TMS component magnitudes show shrinkage, and the paper reports imperfect specialization, including components that partially represent secondary input-feature computations; see R2 and R4.
